note: Rabbi Abba owed money to Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, and they came before the judge Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. Rabbi Abba said he would pay once he got his promissory note back; Rav Yitzhak said he had lost it and offered to write a receipt instead. Rabbi Abba cited Rav and Shmuel, who rule that no receipt is written. The judge said he honored Rav and Shmuel so much he would put their dust on his eyes, but Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish both rule that a receipt is written.
why: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said a receipt is never written when a whole debt is repaid; the Gemara disagrees and brings this case to prove that it is.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: The lender, who had lost the promissory note.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The borrower, who would not pay without getting the note back.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
people.about: The Sage who served as judge in the case.

people.name: Rav and Shmuel
people.about: The two great early Sages of Babylonia, often cited as a pair.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish
people.about: The two great Sages of the Land of Israel in their generation, study partners.

terms.meaning: A written loan document. Normally it is handed back or torn up when the debt is paid, so it cannot be used to collect a second time.
A signed document saying the debt was paid, written for the borrower when the note itself cannot be returned.
